decision_reason: Bareos is a mature and actively distributed open-source network backup and recovery system, but its documented origin is a community developer's fork of Bacula, later stewarded commercially by Bareos GmbH & Co. KG; no government agency is shown to have created, commissioned, funded, sponsored, or stewarded this product. French SILL inclusion and named public-sector customers are discovery/use evidence only, not government provenance. No catalog entry added.

government_provenance.note: Bareos's own history says it is a Bacula fork whose development began in 2010 when community developer Marco van Wieringen collected rejected contributions in his own branch. The project's public-sector deployments (including the Bavarian State Archives) do not establish a government relationship to product creation or stewardship.

public_source.note: The canonical public repository contains the Bareos source. Official docs state that current community and subscription binaries are built from the same source publicly available on GitHub; installation and build guidance are public.

eligible_license.note: The actual license file identifies GNU AGPL version 3 for Bareos code changes to the Bacula source forked in 2013. The repository retains file-specific notices for inherited and third-party files (including GPL and BSD terms), so the product is not represented as uniformly AGPL; the scoped code grants inspected are OSI-approved.

primary_evidence.note: Bareos's customer case study identifies the Bavarian State Archives as using the product for automated archival-data backups. Current official docs provide install and support guidance and publicly distributed community packages; this is operational/notability evidence, not evidence of government origin.

product_identity: Bareos, a network client/server software suite for backup, recovery, and verification of computer data
agency: No government-originating agency identified; origin is community developer Marco van Wieringen, with current commercial stewardship by Bareos GmbH & Co. KG
geography: Germany-based commercial steward; no government-source geography established
license: Primarily GNU AGPL-3.0 for Bareos changes; upstream and third-party files retain their individual notices/licenses, including other OSI-approved grants
status_note: The official Bareos 2019 overview dates the first release to 2013; the GitHub repository's LICENSE independently states that the source forked in June 2013. Current docs describe 25.x releases, public packages, and install/build instructions. A Bavarian State Archives customer reference is treated as third-party use, not provenance. No exact GOSDIR catalog match found.

decision_reason: The assigned repository is the legacy CodeIgniter 3 PHP framework, not CodeIgniter 4. Although CodeIgniter originated at private vendor EllisLab, the official project history says it was acquired and stewarded by the British Columbia Institute of Technology (BCIT) beginning in 2014; the Province of British Columbia classifies BCIT as a public post-secondary institution authorized under provincial legislation. CodeIgniter 3.0 was released under MIT during that stewardship in 2015, with versioned releases and official installation/user guidance. The current project README describes CI3 as a legacy line receiving mostly security maintenance, so it is a maintained legacy product rather than the current mainline. No catalog entry added.

government_provenance.note: The official CodeIgniter credits state that the project was acquired by BCIT in 2014 and became community-maintained; the 2014 project-lead announcement details BCIT hosting the site/forum, transfer of GitHub/social accounts, and project-lead time. BCIT is listed by the Province as a public post-secondary institution authorized under provincial legislation: https://www2.gov.bc.ca/gov/content/education-training/post-secondary-education/find-a-program-or-institution/find-an-institution. I count its documented project stewardship during the CodeIgniter 3 release period as public-institution provenance, not as the original private EllisLab creation.

public_source.note: The assigned public repository explicitly identifies itself as the legacy CodeIgniter 3 source and links official user, installation, and release guidance. The CodeIgniter 4 successor is a separate product/repository and is not used to transfer claims to this CI3 row.

eligible_license.note: The repository's actual root license.txt grants the standard OSI-approved MIT License to the Software. The official CI3 changelog says version 3.0.0, released March 30, 2015, was relicensed from its prior proprietary terms to MIT; this establishes the eligible grant and its source line, while separately licensed dependencies retain their own notices.

primary_evidence.note: This agency-stewarded reusable framework has versioned releases (official changelog lists CI3.1.13, released March 3, 2022) and first-party download, installation, and user-guide documentation. The official repository says CI3 is in maintenance and receives mostly security updates; this is an agency-published software/release-and-guidance notability pathway, not a popularity-only case.

product_identity: CodeIgniter 3 (CI3), a legacy PHP application-development framework/toolkit for building web applications; distinct from the current CodeIgniter 4 line
agency: British Columbia Institute of Technology (BCIT), a British Columbia public post-secondary institution that acquired and stewarded CodeIgniter from 2014 until transition to the separate CodeIgniter Foundation in 2019
license: MIT for the CodeIgniter 3 first-party framework source; official changelog documents the March 30, 2015 relicensing, and repository license.txt contains the full MIT grant
status_note: The earliest public CodeIgniter version dates to 2006 but predates its eligible MIT grant; CI3.0.0 is the first eligible public licensed source line (2015). CI3 is legacy (CI4 is separate), with its current repository README describing security-focused maintenance; repository history shows source activity through 2024-03-19, while 3.1.13 remains the latest published CI3 release. Treat status as Maintained/legacy, not as the current mainline. No exact GOSDIR catalog match found.

decision_reason: Leezenflow is a specific municipal green-wave assistant for cyclists, not merely a vendor product deployed by government: the City of Münster adopted the hackathon idea, built and evaluated a prototype using a Federal Ministry of Transport grant, later expanded the solution through the federal Model Projects Smart Cities program, and contracted bCyber GmbH to program and manufacture the devices. The exact assigned repository is the publicly accessible Python application code identified by the federal Smart City Dialog page, and its README plus LICENSE.txt grant GPL-3.0-or-later. The first public repository commit is dated 2022-01-31 and is titled “public release”; this source year is distinct from the 2019 hackathon idea and May 2021 first on-street test. Current official evidence describes ten installed devices and replication by CityLAB Berlin. No catalog entry added.

government_provenance.note: The federal Smart City Dialog page says Münster's city administration picked up the Münsterhack 2019 idea and implemented a prototype with a grant from the Federal Ministry of Transport and Digital Infrastructure; the municipal Smart City office coordinates it, and bCyber programmed/manufactured the devices. The city later expanded it under the Federal Model Projects Smart Cities program. This is government-funded/commissioned product development, not just public-sector use.

public_source.note: The federal source identifies this exact GitHub repository as the Python code for Leezenflow's traffic-signal phase reading, green-phase arrival prediction, and LED-display behavior. The public repository contains the application, tests, requirements, and setup/production instructions. A separate linked documentation repository covers hardware/build documentation and is not used to claim its different license for this code.

eligible_license.note: The repository README states that this program is licensed under the GNU General Public License version 3 or, at the recipient's option, any later version; the root LICENSE.txt contains the complete GPLv3 text. This grant covers the first-party Python Leezenflow code in this repository; separately linked hardware documentation and third-party libraries have their own terms.

primary_evidence.note: The federal platform's 2025 product-specific page describes the operating municipal system, its ten-device installation in Münster, nine additional sites, user-facing cycling guidance, and ongoing support through the regular traffic-light operation. It also says CityLAB Berlin reused the solution as Kottiflow. This establishes documented operational deployment and independent reuse, not merely a code release or star count.

product_identity: Leezenflow, the Python software for a municipal cyclist green-wave assistant that reads traffic-signal phase data, predicts whether a cyclist can reach the next light on green, and drives roadside LED displays
agency: City of Münster (Stabsstelle Smart City and Amt für Mobilität und Tiefbau); prototype funded by Germany's Federal Ministry of Transport and Digital Infrastructure and later expanded under the Federal Model Projects Smart Cities; bCyber GmbH was the contracted programmer/manufacturer
license: GNU GPL-3.0-or-later for the repository's first-party Python application code
status_note: The first repository commit (2022-01-31, message “public release”) adds the source and GPL license; it is the first defensible public licensed-source year, not the earlier 2019 hackathon or 2021 live test. The latest source commit is 2024-05-21; despite activity being over 24 months old, the federal 2025 source still documents the exact repository, current municipal operation and replication, meeting the maintained-by-current-use exception. The federal page is primary evidence for both sponsorship and current use. No exact GOSDIR catalog match found.

decision_reason: Beekeeper Studio is an active, publicly distributed commercial/community SQL editor and database manager created by an independent two-person development team; no government agency is shown to have authored, commissioned, funded, or stewarded it. The French SILL entry is a catalog/use lead only and does not establish provenance. The assigned repository also mixes GPL community code with paid features under a commercial source-available license, so the exact grant scope for the repository as a whole is unresolved. No catalog entry added.

government_provenance.note: The product's first-party retrospective says the two-person team started work in 2019 and launched Beekeeper Studio in 2020; the company describes it as an independent database app. No public agency creation, funding, commissioning, or stewardship relationship was identified. The French SILL entry is not treated as provenance.

public_source.note: This is the product's canonical public repository and contains substantial client application source, build/packaging files, and documentation links. The README says official desktop binaries are distributed for macOS, Windows, and Linux.

eligible_license.note: The README says most repository code and the Community Edition are GPLv3 but that paid features also exist in this same repository under a commercial source-available license; the official open-source page likewise says only a significant portion is GPL and describes separate paid code. Without a verified component boundary for the exact assigned repository/product scope, do not treat GPL metadata or the Community Edition statement as an OSI grant for the whole repository.

primary_evidence.note: The official product site and docs provide versioned distribution, installation guides for desktop operating systems, connection and usage documentation, and a public Community Edition release path. The team's 2021 retrospective documents adoption/download growth but that popularity metric is not the admission basis; current official distribution plus user guidance establishes a supported user-facing software product.

product_identity: Beekeeper Studio, a cross-platform SQL editor/database manager; the assigned repository contains Community Edition code and also selected paid-edition features, so license scope is mixed
agency: No government-originating agency identified; developed by the independent Beekeeper Studio team and now distributed by Beekeeper Studio, Inc.
geography: No government-source geography identified; global commercial/community software distribution
license: Mixed scope: GPLv3 community code, with paid feature code in the same repository under a commercial source-available license; 2019 root MIT grant history and current file-by-file/product scope require reconciliation for this repository-wide candidate
status_note: The public commit history shows Beekeeper-specific application development in 2019 and a root MIT license added 2019-10-07; an earlier 2015 history belongs to Sqlectron predecessor code, not the Beekeeper Studio product identity. The official retrospective dates public launch to April 2020. Current 2026 release activity and official docs/distribution establish freshness and product identity, but current repository mixes GPL and commercial-source-available paid components. No exact GOSDIR catalog match found.

decision_reason: Gunicorn is a mature, actively maintained Python WSGI/ASGI server with a clear public MIT grant and documented use in Django deployment guidance, but the project describes volunteer maintenance and originates with independent maintainers; no government agency created, commissioned, funded, sponsored, or stewarded this project. French SILL inclusion or public-sector use of a web server would not prove government provenance. No catalog entry added.

government_provenance.note: The project README identifies Gunicorn as a volunteer-maintained server ported from the Ruby Unicorn project and names individual maintainers; no government sponsor/steward is identified. SILL listing is a lead and is not treated as provenance.

public_source.note: The canonical public repository contains the Python WSGI server, install instructions, current development history and official documentation links; source and releases are publicly accessible.

eligible_license.note: The actual root LICENSE grants the standard OSI-approved MIT License to the software and associated documentation, with copyright notices for Benoît Chesneau and Paul J. Davis. The README confirms this grant for Gunicorn; the exact MIT text is present.

primary_evidence.note: Django's official, current deployment documentation has a dedicated integration guide for this exact server, gives the install command and shows how it serves a Django WSGI application. Current Gunicorn releases and installation/deployment documentation show continued maintained distribution; this is documented independent framework reuse, separate from government provenance.

product_identity: Gunicorn (Green Unicorn), a Python pre-fork WSGI HTTP server for UNIX with current ASGI worker support
agency: No government-originating agency identified; independently maintained by Benoît Chesneau and volunteer contributors
geography: Global Python/Unix project; no government-source geography identified
license: MIT for the Gunicorn software and associated documentation, as stated by the project README and granted in the root LICENSE
status_note: The official distribution history shows Gunicorn 0.1 published on 2010-01-03; the official changelog begins with 2010 versions and the repository README says the server has powered Python apps since 2010. Current official changelog shows 2026 releases, and Django maintains product-specific deployment instructions. No exact GOSDIR catalog match found.
